steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell J, then A, then N with the two-handed BSL alphabet, keeping the flow smooth.
Let your dominant hand work over the steady non-dominant base hand for each letter.
Mouth the word 'January' as you fingerspell so your reader catches the month.
tip: BSL has no lexical sign for months — every British signer fingerspells them, J-A-N included.

steps: Form a closed flat hand with both hands, fingers pressed together.
Rest your dominant hand directly on top of your non-dominant hand at chest height.
Slide the top hand backwards until it lands on your non-dominant forearm in one smooth motion.
Keep both palms facing down while the base hand stays steady throughout the slide.
Mouth the word 'before' clearly as the top hand arrives at your forearm.
tip: The top hand physically moves backward — the direction of the movement carries the meaning.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of you in an open flat shape, fingers together.
Turn both palms to face upward, holding the hands level with each other.
Bounce both hands up and down together in unison, repeating the motion steadily.
Keep your palms facing up the whole time, the two hands mirroring each other exactly.
Mouth 'today' distinctly while you bounce — the mouth pattern separates it from NOW.
tip: The manual form matches NOW; the mouthed word 'today' is what pins it to today.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady as the base hand in front of you.
Fingerspell D, then E, then C with the two-handed BSL alphabet in one smooth run.
Keep the letters tight and connected so the abbreviation reads clearly.
Mouth 'December' as you finish the final C.
tip: Short months get three letters: D-E-C covers December for every British signer.

steps: Close both hands into fists with only the index fingers extended straight.
Hold your non-dominant fist out in front of you with the forearm pointing outward.
Start your dominant fist at the elbow end of your non-dominant forearm.
Slide the dominant fist along the forearm until the two fists meet.
Keep both palms facing sideways and mouth 'week' as the fists touch.
tip: One slide marks out the length of a week along your arm — seven days, one sweep.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space at chest height.
Fingerspell J-U-N-E with the two-handed BSL alphabet, flowing from letter to letter.
Work your dominant hand over your non-dominant base hand without pausing.
Mouth 'June' clearly as the spelling completes.
tip: Short months are spelled in full — four quick letters, J-U-N-E, with no abbreviation.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady as your base hand.
Fingerspell O, then C, then T using the two-handed BSL alphabet.
Keep the three letters flowing in one continuous, unbroken motion.
Mouth 'October' as you land on the final T.
tip: O-C-T is the accepted BSL form — the month lives in the fingerspelling, not a sign.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell M, then A, then R with the two-handed BSL alphabet in a smooth flow.
Keep your non-dominant base hand steady while the dominant hand forms each letter.
Mouth 'March' distinctly as the spelling finishes.
tip: M-A-R is the standard BSL form — same abbreviation convention as every other month.

steps: Hold both hands up in the fingerspelling space at chest height.
Fingerspell S, then E, then P with the two-handed BSL alphabet, flowing smoothly.
Keep the letters connected so the abbreviation reads as one unit.
Mouth 'September' as you finish the P.
tip: S-E-P is standard, though some signers add the T — Sept and Sep are both understood.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell J-U-L-Y with the two-handed BSL alphabet in one fluid run.
Let your dominant hand shape each letter over the steady base hand.
Mouth 'July' clearly as the final Y completes.
tip: Short months are spelled in full — J-U-L-Y, the whole word, with no shortcuts.

steps: Raise your dominant hand and form a V shape with your index and middle fingers.
Hold the V hand in front of your body at chest height, palm facing sideways.
Twist your wrist so the fingertips rock back and forth in small repeated swings.
Keep the movement tight and rhythmic, repeating it two or three times.
Pair it with a neutral expression and mouth 'again' as the V rocks.
tip: The rocking V replays the same motion — repetition is built into the sign itself.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady in front of you as the base hand.
Fingerspell A-P-R-I-L with the two-handed BSL alphabet, keeping the letters flowing.
Move your dominant hand smoothly from one letter to the next without stopping.
Mouth 'April' as you complete the final L.
tip: Longer month names are spelled out in full — A-P-R-I-L rides the fingerspelling alphabet.

steps: Hold both hands in a closed flat shape, fingers pressed firmly together.
Raise them in front of your chest with both palms facing toward you.
Sweep your dominant hand up slightly, then brush it swiftly downward across your non-dominant palm.
Make the downward brush quick and decisive, ending just below the base hand.
Shake your head firmly once as the hand brushes down, mouthing 'never'.
tip: The sharp downward brush 'wipes out' the idea — a definite no to every time.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell A, then U, then G with the two-handed BSL alphabet in a smooth flow.
Keep your base hand still while the dominant hand shapes each letter.
Mouth 'August' distinctly as the G lands.
tip: A-U-G is the standard abbreviation — three letters, fingerspelled, no lexical sign needed.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady as the base hand at chest height.
Fingerspell F, then E, then B with the two-handed BSL alphabet.
Keep the letters tight and flowing in one continuous movement.
Mouth 'February' as you finish the B.
tip: F-E-B follows the same three-letter abbreviation pattern as January's J-A-N.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat in front of you, palm facing upward.
Make a clenched fist with your dominant hand, thumb extended outward.
Rest the dominant fist directly on top of the open base palm.
Brush the fist back and forth across the palm repeatedly, knuckles grazing it.
Keep the brushing steady and unbroken, mouthing 'always' throughout.
tip: The never-stopping brush is the point — ALWAYS means the action does not end.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm stiffly in front of you with a closed flat hand.
Raise your dominant hand in a closed flat shape, held vertically above the other.
Bring the dominant hand down and land it firmly on your non-dominant forearm.
Keep the landing single and decided, palm facing down on contact.
Mouth 'early' as the hand lands, with a matter-of-fact expression.
tip: The hand lands high and early on the arm — the sign arrives before the wrist does.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady in front of you at chest height.
Form the fingerspelled letter F with your dominant hand above the base hand.
Move the dominant fingers in a small circular motion over the stationary base hand.
Keep the circles tight and repeated, palm facing down toward the base hand.
Mouth 'Friday' clearly while you circle the F.
tip: Some signers tap the F twice instead of circling — both forms mean Friday.

steps: Make a closed fist with your dominant hand, index finger pointing straight up.
Hold the hand in front of your body at chest height.
Move the hand across your body while tilting your wrist from side to side.
Keep the index finger pointing upward through the whole sideways journey.
Mouth 'later' as you move, with a relaxed, unhurried expression.
tip: The finger waggles its way across your body — pushed into the future, not now.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and steady as your base hand.
Form the fingerspelled letter M with your dominant hand above it.
Tap the M down onto the base palm twice in quick succession.
Keep the base hand still, palm facing up, while the M bounces off it.
Mouth 'Monday' clearly on the double tap.
tip: One M, two taps — Monday is the only weekday that double-taps a single letter.
